title: Battle of Yeongcheon (1950): The Turning Point at the Perimeter
subtitle: September 5 – 13, 1950

lines: 1 a.m., September 5th, 1950. A mountain valley north of Yeongcheon.
In the pouring rain, five North Korean tanks began rolling south.
s01.label: Dramatization

lines: Yeongcheon was a crossroads: the Taegu–Pohang road met the road south to Gyeongju.
If it broke here, the waist of the Naktong line would be cut clean through.
callouts: TAEGU – YEONGCHEON – POHANG · YEONGCHEON – GYEONGJU – PUSAN

lines: Turn west, and the troops fighting at Dabu-dong would be hit from behind.
Push south to Gyeongju, and almost nothing stood between the enemy and Pusan.
Then, on September 6th, North Korean troops entered the town of Yeongcheon.
The waist of the Naktong line had finally been pierced.
Yet one week later, the North Korean division that took Yeongcheon would vanish from the map.
This is the Battle of Yeongcheon, the hidden reversal that held the line.
s05.title: Battle of Yeongcheon
s05.sub: The Turning Point at the Perimeter · 1950

lines: By August 1950, South Korean and UN forces had been pushed back to the Naktong River.
From Masan through Waegwan to Yeongdeok, it was their last line of defense.
chapter: THE WAIST OF THE LAST LINE

lines: All through August, the North Koreans went for Taegu, and were stopped at Dabu-dong.
So in September, they turned their eyes east.
s07.label: ROK soldiers on the Naktong line (Aug 1950)

lines: The attack fell to the North Korean 15th Division.
It came down through Uiseong and over the ridges of Mount Bohyeon, heading south for Yeongcheon.
North of Yeongcheon lies rugged high ground, Mount Bohyeon at 1,124 meters, and Mount Giryong.
Come down off those mountains, and a wide basin opens up along the Geumho River.
s09.title: Yeongcheon · North–South Terrain Profile

lines: The town of Yeongcheon sat in the middle of that basin, on the banks of the Geumho.
For an enemy that had crossed the mountains, no terrain was left to stop him.
Holding the line here was the ROK 8th Division.
Worn out, it had fought its way south through the central mountains since day one.
s11.label: ROK soldiers on the march (1950)

lines: The North Korean 15th Division attacked behind its tanks.
The South Korean division did not have a single tank of its own.
callouts: ROK records: 5 tanks led the attack

lines: Meanwhile, the North Koreans were attacking along the entire Naktong front.
Masan, Waegwan, Dabu-dong, Pohang. Nowhere could the defenders spare a single man.
On the night of September 2nd, the North Korean attack began.
By dawn the next day, the positions of the ROK 16th Regiment had collapsed.
s13.label: Dramatization

lines: The 8th Division fell back to the Giryong ridge and dug a new line.
But before dawn on September 5th, the enemy struck from three directions at once.
The tanks led the way through the rain.
When an enemy tank swung in behind the line, an entire ROK regiment scattered in moments.
s15.label: Dramatization

lines: Korean officers and American advisors rounded up the scattered men.
Regrouped, the 8th Division turned to face Yeongcheon once more.
s15b.label: ROK soldier on watch in a trench (1950)

lines: On September 6th, the North Koreans pushed into the town of Yeongcheon.
The road linking Taegu and Pohang had fallen into enemy hands.
South of town the enemy set a roadblock and cut the road to Gyeongju.
By Korean records, the road between Yeongcheon and Gyeongju stayed closed for five days.
callouts: YEONGCHEON–GYEONGJU ROAD CUT 5 DAYS · ROK RECORDS

lines: Then ROK Army headquarters and the U.S. Eighth Army made an urgent call.
Pull regiments out of other sectors, and send them to Yeongcheon.
s18.label: Dramatization

lines: The 1st Division's 11th Regiment, the 6th's 19th, and the new 7th Division's 5th.
Regiments from across the front raced to Yeongcheon by truck.
Command went to the ROK II Corps commander, General Yu Jae-hung.
A platoon of American tanks came too, but the heart of the fight was South Korean infantry.
s20.label: ROK troops moving by truck (1950)
callouts: ROK records: 1 U.S. tank platoon (5 tanks)

lines: From the afternoon of September 6th, the town changed hands in a seesaw fight.
Each time the ROK troops retook it, fresh enemy units pushed back in.
s21.label: Dramatization

lines: On September 7th, the 19th Regiment ambushed an enemy supply column, wrecking some thirty trucks.
The enemy's forward infantry was being cut off from the supplies behind it.
Then, at 2:45 p.m. on September 8th,
South Korean troops finally took the town of Yeongcheon back.
Now the hunter and the hunted traded places.
The enemy deep in Yeongcheon was now trapped among South Korean forces.
s23.sub: The enemy that broke in, surrounded in turn

lines: The 15th Division's artillery had run ahead of its infantry, and was out of shells.
Korean records say on September 9th, the ROK 5th Regiment overran an enemy artillery regiment hiding in a tunnel.
s24.label: Dramatization

lines: On September 10th, ROK II Corps launched its general counterattack.
It reopened the Gyeongju road and closed in from the south, west and north.
The 21st and 19th Regiments blocked the paths back into the mountains.
The enemy that had come down to Yeongcheon now had no way home.
Prisoner interrogations revealed the location of the enemy division headquarters.
On September 11th, ROK troops struck it at Daeui-dong, north of Yeongcheon.
s27.label: North Korean prisoners taken by ROK troops (Sep 1950)

lines: South Korean shells rained down on the headquarters hidden in an apple orchard.
U.S. records say the division's chief of staff, Colonel Kim Yon, was killed around then.
s28.label: Dramatization
callouts: U.S. Army history: Chief of Staff Col. Kim Yon KIA (Sep 9–10)

lines: Its commander, Pak Song-chol, had reportedly already been relieved for the delay.
Leaderless, the enemy abandoned tanks and guns and scattered into the hills.
That same Pak Song-chol would later become premier of North Korea.
s29.label: Dramatization

lines: On September 12th, the 8th Division restored its broken line.
And by September 13th, the threat to Yeongcheon was gone.
s30.label: Dramatization

lines: By Korean records, 3,799 North Koreans killed and 309 captured.
Five tanks destroyed, and 85 vehicles and 2,327 small arms captured.
The North Korean 15th Division had effectively ceased to exist as a division.
A rare victory: a South Korean-led counterattack broke an entire enemy division.
s32.label: Abandoned North Korean T-34 tank (1950)

lines: How could a South Korean force without tanks destroy an entire enemy division?
Let's break it down into four factors.
s33.head: No Tanks vs Tank-Led Enemy — How?

lines: First, rapid redeployment.
s34.title: Rapid Redeployment

lines: Regiments were pulled from across the front and massed at Yeongcheon within a day or two.
The very afternoon the enemy entered town, they were already arriving.
The U.S. Army's official history called it a notable command achievement.
Second, the collapse of enemy supply.
s36.title: Enemy Supply Collapse

lines: The enemy had crossed rugged mountains and gone too far; shells and food could not keep up.
Even after taking the town, he had no strength left for the next step.
Third, counter-encirclement.
s38.title: Counter-Encirclement

lines: The ROK troops didn't just plug the gap; they swung behind the enemy and cut his escape.
A battle to hold became a battle to trap.
Fourth, the artillery strike.
s40.title: Artillery Strike

lines: South Korean artillery first silenced the enemy's guns,
then hit the orchard where the enemy headquarters was hiding.
s41.label: ROK artillery in action (1950)

lines: Two days after the battle, on September 15th, UN forces landed at Inchon.
Because the Naktong line held, the door to the counteroffensive swung open.
On September 16th, the forces on the Naktong front broke out as well.
After nearly three months of retreat, the tide of the war turned for the first time.
s43.label: UN forces landing at Inchon (Sep 15, 1950)

lines: Today, a battle monument and a memorial park stand in Yeongcheon.
And nearby, at the Yeongcheon National Cemetery, countless veterans lie at rest.
s44.label: Yeongcheon National Cemetery

lines: More than seventy years have passed since then.
Few remember Yeongcheon the way they remember Dabu-dong or Inchon.
Yet without those nine days, the September counteroffensive might never have come.
Nine days that held the waist of the Naktong line, at its most dangerous moment.
Yeongcheon was where the great counteroffensive began.
